title: Richard Gadd, Bill Camp and Ray McKinnon Join Michael Keaton-Directed Western ‘Rode to Ruin’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Emmy Award-winning actor and writer Richard Gadd, multi-Emmy and SAG nominated actor Bill Camp and Oscar-nominated filmmaker and actor Ray McKinnon
body:
Emmy Award-winning actor and writer Richard Gadd, multi-Emmy and SAG nominated actor Bill Camp and Oscar-nominated filmmaker and actor Ray McKinnon are joining “Rode to Ruin,” a Western thriller directed by Michael Keaton.

	Keaton also stars in the film, which is now in production in Santa Fe, New Mexico, along with Morgan Freeman and Laura Linney. Angel acquired worldwide rights and will release “Rode to Ruin” in theaters in 2027.


	Also joining the cast are Chris Candy, Travis Hammer, Thom Rivera and Derek Hinkey. 
	

	“Richard, Ray and Bill are the kind of actors who make every scene better simply by being in it,” said producer Lori McCreary. “They each bring such specificity, humanity and truth to their work, and seeing them alongside Michael, Morgan and Laura is incredibly exciting. Avy Kaufman has helped us make this cast something very special.”

	The story follows a retired U.S. Marshal whose 40-year search for his wife’s killer leads him to an aging outlaw losing his memory, and to a buried truth neither man may survive, according to the synopsis.

	Gadd plays Clive McKinney, the young, dangerous, and charismatic head of an outlaw gang riding the territory in search of a rumored fortune and the man who destroyed his family. 

	“Rode to Ruin” is produced by McCreary, Keaton, Kelly Mendelsohn, Gary Lucchesi and Richard Gray for Freeman and McCreary’s Revelations Entertainment and Keaton’s George and Leona Productions.

	R. Dean McCreary wrote the screenplay, and executive producers include Steve Sarowitz, Carter Boehm, Skip Herman, Blake Johnson, Randall Emmett and John Bommarito.
	

	Gadd is represented by UTA, Individual Artist Management and Casarotto and Markham, Froggatt & Irwin. Camp is represented by UTA and Franklin, Weinrib, Rudell & Vassallo, P.C. McKinnon is represented by Paradigm, Anonymous Content and Skrzyniarz & Mallean.

	Linney is represented by CAA, Lighthouse Management + Media, and Kevin Yorn; Keaton is represented by CAA and JSSK and Morgan Freeman is represented by CAA and Sloane, Offer, Weber and Dern.

title: Peter Chan Rules Out AI-Generated Content, Says Feature Films Will Survive the Rise of Vertical Dramas
description: Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun, director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his fi
body:
Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun, director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his filmmaking but “definitely not AIGC,” or AI-generated content, and that the two-hour feature will hold its ground against short-form and vertical dramas, at least in his lifetime.

	Speaking at an In Conversation event at the Singapore International Film Festival, Chan was asked by an audience member whether he had ever doubted his decision to go into the film industry. His advice to aspiring filmmakers: “This is probably the toughest time for film, but do I believe this medium is going to be lost and gone to short-form entertainment? No.”
	

	He said he would probably use AI as a technique, the way the industry already uses CGI and special effects, noting that CGI has relied on AI for years without calling it that. “Anything that helps me make movies, I welcome. But they won’t know art. Movies are still made by people,” Chan said.


	Young audiences’ shrinking attention spans have them turning to short and vertical dramas, Chan said, while at the other end, people are listening to podcasts that run for hours, and Christopher Nolan did podcasts around the world to explain his purist approach of making “Oppenheimer” the way movies were made in the ’50s. “So there are two completely opposite ends of the spectrum that are surviving and thriving simultaneously. So I believe that movie will be around for a long, long time,” he told a rapt audience at the Grand Ballroom, Marina Bay Sands.

	Chan’s latest film, “The Road Not Taken,” premiered in Toronto. “My new movie is about Alzheimer’s, but it’s really not just about Alzheimer’s. It’s about a broken family that has all sorts of problems a family could have,” he said.
	

	The story centers on a couple in the middle of divorce proceedings when the wife, who has early-onset Alzheimer’s, no longer remembers the divorce and drifts back in her mind to the time they fell in love in their 20s. A harsh grandfather and the couple’s relationship with their Gen Z daughter complete the picture. The daughter in the film is 20, the same age as Chan’s own daughter, who is training to become an actor. Chan’s partner is actor Sandra Ng.

	The English title comes from the Robert Frost poem, which Chan called his life motto, while the Chinese title, “Ming Tian Hui Geng Hao,” translates as “Tomorrow Will Be Better.” “There’s really no right path,” he said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, it’s all about how you walk it. You make it right.”

	While researching the film, Chan visited an Alzheimer’s care institution in Chengdu, in China’s Sichuan province, where he picked up an eight-word Mandarin phrase that he used to sum up his career: go with the flow, and know when to stop. In the ’90s, when he was making romantic comedies at United Filmmakers Organization (UFO), the company he co-founded, gangster pictures and wuxia ruled Hong Kong screens. “We were not exactly going with the flow, but we did make the flow, somehow,” he said.

	That same flow later carried him to “The Warlords,” which he described as his biggest film. “Never had I thought that I would ever make a historical epic battle movie with Jet Li. That was never, ever in my agenda for my entire life,” Chan said.

	This year marks the 30th anniversary of “Comrades,” which Chan made at 34 as his seventh feature and which captures Hong Kong between 1985 and 1995. He left Hong Kong on Christmas Eve 1996, and only after returning from America around two and a half years later did he grasp how deeply the film had affected filmmakers in mainland China, South Korea and Southeast Asia, even though, he said, it probably only barely recouped its investment.

	“That movie gave me a lease of movie life for the next 30 years, until now,” Chan said.

	He said 90% of people remember him for that single film, “as if I have not done better afterwards,” calling it a blessing but also a spell he wanted to break.

	Chan, who also said the ’90s marked the start of Hong Kong cinema’s decline rather than its golden age, described his DreamWorks film “The Love Letter” as a difficult experience. He was not thrown by working across cultures, he said, having grown up Thai-Chinese and feeling like an outsider even in Hong Kong. What he struggled with was a corporate system where it was unclear who called the shots, and a reliance on test screenings that he likened to today’s algorithms. He said he was probably the first, if not the only, Hong Kong filmmaker to make a non-action film inside the U.S. studio system.
	

	“Had I gone to America or Hollywood with the knowledge that I have of film and marketing and dealing with corporate, I probably would have fared better,” Chan said. “I was too young then, too naive.”

	Asked later by an audience member how he navigates censorship in mainland China, Chan said: “Dealing with a corporate is very, very difficult. And if I can survive that, I can survive anything.” He added that limitations of budget, stars, studios or censorship tend to push filmmakers to be more creative.

	After Hollywood, Chan set up Applause Pictures, a pan-Asian venture that made 10 films in two and a half years, most of them horror. Its output included “The Eye” franchise and the “Three” horror omnibus films, which brought together directors including Park Chan-wook, Miike Takashi, Kim Jee-woon and Fruit Chan. He also executive produced “One Fine Spring Day” for Korean director Hur Jin-ho – director of SGIFF opener “The Assassin(s)” – whose debut “Christmas in August” he loved. But a planned three-part love story with Hur and Japan’s Iwai Shunji found no investors.

	“If we continue this pan-Asian effort, I’m going to be stuck with making horror films my whole life,” Chan said of the decision to move on to mainland China, where his first film was the 2005 musical “Perhaps Love.”

	An aspiring screenwriter in the audience asked how he handles a scene that isn’t landing. “I don’t usually fix it for them. I make them fix it over and over and over and over again,” Chan said, adding that after saying “great” to everything at home, he doesn’t do the same with his writers.

	He credited nine writers on “The Warlords,” and said screenwriters joke that his films’ writers would not fit in a minibus. “I milk the writer to death, and then I milk another writer,” he said. “So the writers’ community really don’t like me very much. But making movies is not about being well-liked.”

	Though he is often seen as a genre-hopper, Chan said the same concerns run through his work, citing the love triangles in his debut “Alan & Eric: Between Hello and Goodbye,” “Comrades,” “Perhaps Love” and even “The Warlords,” which he called a love triangle between three brothers.
	

	“Making every movie is answering some sort of life questions that I have at that stage, in point of my life,” he said. “So in a way, I’ve been making the same movie in my mind in the last 36 years.”

title: ‘Ebenezer’ Creates a Real Venmo Profile for Scrooge, Which Hands Out Money and Accepts It, Too
description:
The surly miser Ebenezer Scrooge is no longer just a fictional character haunting the holidays — he’s on Venmo.

	To promote Ti West’s upcoming ada
body:
The surly miser Ebenezer Scrooge is no longer just a fictional character haunting the holidays — he’s on Venmo.

	To promote Ti West’s upcoming adaptation of the notorious character in the film “Ebenezer,” starring Johnny Depp in the titular role, the Paramount promotional team created a Venmo account for Ebenezer Scrooge. The official account for the film announced the news on X, writing, “Ebenezer Scrooge is now on @venmo. Think he’s feeling generous? 💰 Send a request: https://venmo.com/u/EBENEZERmovie” accompanied by a video of people making requests for various amounts of money and Scrooge’s stingy payouts. Despite the request, Ebenezer’s response is always the same, giving just a penny in return.
	

	An error message reading, “We’re sorry the transaction could not be completed. Please contact the person you’re trying to pay” appeared when two Variety staffers tried to request some money. A source close to promotion confirmed that the Venmo has been working — it just grew so popular with requests that it temporarily caused a jam in the system and is being fixed.


	Although Scrooge’s Venmo is dishing out money, he also appears to be accepting it. The public feed of his account is filled with payments made out to him. “For cheers and joy! (And maybe a little luck please)” one benefactor wrote. Another wrote, “$ Retainer Fee — for the Ghost of Christmas Past to haunt my exes with a little bah humbug spirit.” Several others paid Scrooge to boost his Christmas spirit.

	It is unclear where this sent money will actually end up.
	

	Paramount Pictures’ “Ebenezer” will hit theaters on Nov. 13. The official logline reads: “The name you know, the story you don’t.” Judging from the trailer, West — known for directing the horror trilogy “X” — is zooming in on the darker aspects of Charles Dickens’ beloved story, showing Depp’s character being haunted by some seriously scary ghosts and getting buried alive.

	Depp stars alongside Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen. Based on “A Christmas Carol” by Charles Dickens, Nathaniel Halpern adapted the screenplay.

	“Ebenezer” marks Depp’s return home to Hollywood for the holidays as his first major movie since his highly publicized 2022 trial against ex-wife Amber Heard. Both Depp and Heard accused the other of domestic abuse and defamation during their relationship, with Depp ultimately awarded $10 million in compensatory damages and $5 million in punitive damages from Heard, while Heard was awarded $2 million in compensatory damages. His last major Hollywood studio film was “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald” in 2018.

Oct 22, 2026 5:10pm PT	
	

	
	Oscars Predictions 2027: Is ‘You Can See Everything’ the Film That Can Take Down ‘The Odyssey’?
	



			
			
	
						

									A24
	
					


							
		

	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.



	

					“The Odyssey”
									Universal Pictures
	




	2027 Academy Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Oct. 22, 2026): Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to a staggering $15 million over the weekend, a number most nonfiction films never see in a full run. It’s also boasting a record-setting 99 on Metacritic, 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and holding a 4.7 (out of 5) on Letterboxd and 9.4 on IMDb.

	What if the first documentary nominated for best picture goes all the way to the top prize?

	A few studios are trying to frame the race as David vs. Goliath regarding how they can possibly topple Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar sensation “The Odyssey.” What if this is actually Odysseus vs. Elizabeth Holmes?

	In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture (Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose and Jack Davis), director (Fielder and Oppenheim), production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian).

	Variety confirmed exclusively after the film made its surprise world premiere (and general existence became known) at the Telluride Film Festival that Amanda Seyfried, credited in the film as Elizabeth Holmes, is eligible for the Academy Awards in the acting categories. Seyfried, who also appears as herself while reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. If she lands the nomination, it would be her second, following “Mank” (2020). She would get there for playing two people at once: herself and the woman she already won an Emmy statue for playing. Christopher Abbott, who also appears in the film as Holmes’ spouse, Billy Evans, in recreated scenes, is also eligible for acting consideration in the supporting actor category. Fielder, credited as himself, may be eligible to submit as a performer, but Variety has confirmed he won’t.

	No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture in 98 ceremonies. The zeitgeist says this one can be. 

	The race is getting very exciting.

	In other news, Variety has confirmed that Lionsgate’s bid to have its Michael Jackson biopic compete as a comedy or musical at the Golden Globes has been denied. The Golden Globes’ decision means the film, starring Jaafar Jackson as the King of Pop, is currently slated for the drama categories where it would compete for one of the six available slots against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and more. The supporting actor and actress categories do not separate by genre, so this has no effect on his co-stars Colman Domingo and Nia Long.

	This week’s updates are below.

	The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.

title: John Mayer Sets Up His Own Label, Sob Rock Records, in Partnership With Mercury to Release First New Solo Music in Five Years
description: John Mayer has had his hands full with what felt like a hundred projects over the past few years — with putting out new music not among them. It ta
body:
John Mayer has had his hands full with what felt like a hundred projects over the past few years — with putting out new music not among them. It takes a stretch of the memory to even recall that he announced a parting of ways with Sony Music back in 2022, with no followup revelation about where, if anywhere, he planned to go next . Now, after hinting at the beginning of this year that new studio recordings were afoot, he’s finally publicly kicking the recording artist part of his career back into gear.
	

	Mayer and associates announced Thursday that he has started up his own label, Sob Rock Records — which shares the name of the last album he put out for Sony, 2021’s “Sob Rock” — to be operated in partnership with Universal Music’s Mercury Records. No album has yet been announced, but his first single in five years, “Tom and Jerry,” is arriving under his new shingle Friday.


	“Working with Tyler Arnold and the talented team at Mercury Records has already proven to be a great partnership,” Mayer said in a statement. “The path from creative vision to execution has never been easier or more rewarding. I feel very inspired, and I’m excited for what’s to come.”

	“John Mayer is one of the greatest artists of all time,” said Arnold, Mercury’s chairman-CEO, and I couldn’t be prouder to welcome him to Mercury Records. We’re excited to be part of his next chapter and to partner with his label, Sob Rock Records, to help bring his creative vision to life.”

	The new single arrives at DSPs at the usual midnight hour as Thursday turns into Friday, but listeners to the artist’s SiriusXM channel, Life With John Mayer, will get a preview throughout the day Thursday. The song was produced by Blake Slatkin with Mayer and mixed by Serban Genhea.
	

	It almost goes without saying that the credits acknowledge the song was recorded at Chaplin Studios. One of Mayer’s biggest endeavors in the past couple of years was joining forces with the film director McG to purchase the Hollywood lot that started as Charlie Chaplin’s studio and eventually became the home of A&M, then Henson Studios. Mayer and McG shared their experience with taking the reins of the studio with Variety at the top of 2026; read about that here. 

	The singer-songwriter-guitarist indicated then that 2026 would mark a turn back toward his solo recording career after several years of focusing on his role as co-frontman of Dead & Company, including being the primary designer of both of that group’s residencies at Sphere in 2024 and 2025.

	Mayer was already known to be coming back as a live performing artist in a big way with a run of shows booked for Sphere in Las Vegas next year. He currently has concerts at the venue booked for April 8 through June 12, all of them in a configuration that will see him doing separate sets with his full band, with the John Mayer Trio and as a solo performer.

title: Michael Gray, Star of ‘Shazam!’ TV Series, Dies at 75
description:
Michael Gray, the star of the 1970s “Shazam!” television series, died on Friday in Palm Desert from natural causes. He was 75.

	Gray first got his
body:
Michael Gray, the star of the 1970s “Shazam!” television series, died on Friday in Palm Desert from natural causes. He was 75.

	Gray first got his break in television in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s “The Little People” alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares. Early in his career, he held several supporting roles across series including playing Marcia’s boyfriend Jeff on “The Brady Bunch” as well as appearing on “Dynasty,” “Marcus Welby, M.D.,” “Room 222” and “The Flying Nun,” as well in films such as “Run, Simon, Run,” “Beyond the Valley of the Dolls” and “Myra Breckinridge.”
	

	In 1974, he joined the cast of “Shazam!” as Billy Batson, starring alongside John Davey and Les Tremayne in the series, which ran for three seasons until 1976. Gray became a teen idol, frequently appearing on the covers of Tiger Beat and other teen magazines.


	“From my very first day on ‘Shazam!,’ Mike and Les [Tremayne] welcomed me like a king,” Davey said about Gray. “Mike was just a loving, sweet guy with a great sense of humor. He loved acting, loved doing the show and, in recent years, loved appearing at comic cons. He really enjoyed meeting and chatting with the fans. Mike was a wonderful man. I don’t think he ever stopped smiling.”

	“Shazam!” was remastered in 2012 for distribution on DVD, which sparked a career resurgence for Gray. In recent years, he appeared in several episodes of the FX series “Archer” as one of the titular character’s boyhood idols, as well as appearing in “Surge of Power” on AMC’s “Comic Book Men.” When “Shazam! Fury of the Gods” released in 2023, Gray made a brief cameo where he interacted with Zachary Levi’s Captain Marvel as a nod to the original series.
	

	Gray was born in Chicago on Sept. 2, 1951, and was raised in Miami Beach, Florida, before moving to Los Angeles to study acting at the Pasadena Playhouse and pursue his career in entertainment. After landing his role in “Shazam!,” Gray began to feel typecast and took a hiatus from acting. During this time, he worked in children’s theater education and men’s fashion, as well as owning and operating a floral business with his wife, Stacy.

	Following the 2012 resurgence of “Shazam!,” Gray frequently attended fan conventions and reconnected with his fanbase while also pursuing roles in projects such as the “Surge of Power” franchise.

	“I meet people [everyday] who say, ‘You have no idea what you did for me as a child.’ ‘You helped me get through life.’ ‘You made me the better man, or woman, that I am today,’” Gray told Fanboy Planet in 2012. “And that’s a nice feeling. I didn’t know the show had that much strength and power back then.”

	Gray is survived by his wife, Stacy Benon Gray, whom he married in 1994; step-children Ryan Cooper and Laurel Cooper; and son-in-law Lee Barker.

title: CBS Premiere Week Multiplatform Ratings See Big Year-Over-Year Increases (EXCLUSIVE)
description: CBS kicked off its fall 2026 TV season the week of Oct. 4 with a strong performance for its new and returning series, according to Nielsen live+7 m
body:
CBS kicked off its fall 2026 TV season the week of Oct. 4 with a strong performance for its new and returning series, according to Nielsen live+7 multiplatform data.

	Per that data, CBS’ premiere week averaged 8.63 million viewers — up 14% from its premiere week in 2025 (the week of Oct. 12). Leading the charge was the return of “Marshals,” which was the No. 1 entertainment show for the week (15.14 million viewers) in both linear and streaming. That was followed by “Tracker,” with 13.86 million viewers. “Marshals” and “Tracker” were also the week’s two most-watched shows in streaming alone.
	

	Meanwhile, “Sheriff Country,” returning for a second season, hit a new series high, with 10.518 viewers — up 27% from its series premiere last year — and “NCIS” returned with 10.59 million viewers for its Season 24 premiere, up 23% from its season premiere last year.


	Overall, if you take out sports, CBS reports pulling off seven of the week’s top 10 series in L+7 multiplatform viewing across linear and streaming. That includes “Marshals,” “Tracker,” “60 Minutes,” “NCIS,” “Sheriff Country,” “NCIS: New York” and “FBI.” When just broadcast is tallied, CBS has eight of the top 10 shows, with “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” also in the mix.

	Besides “NCIS” and “Sheriff Country,” other shows with year-to-year growth during CBS’ premiere week included “NCIS: New York” (up 58% from last year’s time period premiere for “NCIS: Origins,” to 10.52 million), “FBI” (up 18% to 8.93 million), “Georgie & Mandy’s First Wedding” (up 11% to 8.70 million), “Fire Country” (up 7% to 7.96 million), “Survivor” (up 13% to 7.94 million), “NCIS: Origins” (up 19% to 7.75 million), “Elsbeth” (up 5% to 7.69 million), “The Amazing Race” (up 6% to 4.82 million) and “Harlan Coben’s Final Twist” (up 29% to 3.15 million).
	

	Meanwhile, among new series, “Cupertino” saw a big lift in delayed viewing, averaging 7.17 million viewers in L+7 multiplatform — up from 3.19 million in live+same day.

title: Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year
description: Singer-songwriter and Variety Hitmakers 2024 honoree Raye has won the 2026 Mercury prize for her epic second studio album, “This Music May Contain
body:
Singer-songwriter and Variety Hitmakers 2024 honoree Raye has won the 2026 Mercury prize for her epic second studio album, “This Music May Contain Hope,” beating out Olivia Dean, Paul McCartney and others for the prize.

	The Mercury Prize has no real equivalent in the U.S., and is intended to recognize music from the U.K. and Ireland; the Brit Awards are more of a British equivalent to the Grammys. Past Mercury Prize best album winners include Arlo Parks, Little Simz, the XX, James Blake and others.
	

	Raye’s album topped fellow nominees Dave (for “The Boy Who Played the Harp”), Dove Ellis (“Blizzard”). Florence + the Machine (“Everybody Scream”), Jade (“That’s Showbiz Baby!”), Knats (“A Great Day in Newcastle”), Kojey Radical (“Don’t Look Down”), Nia Archives (“Emotional Junglist”), Olivia Dean (“The Art of Loving”), Paul McCartney (“The Boys of Dungeon Lane”), Suede (“Antidepressants”) and the War Child “Help(2)” compilation.


	Variety wrote of Raye’s album: “Suffice it to say, the album does not lack for ambition: Divided into four sections based on the seasons, it sprawls across a surprisingly fast-moving 70 minutes, 17 songs and nearly as many styles. Inevitably, it runs the risk of being too much for some listeners: too many songs, too many stylistic pivots, too much of… well, basically everything. This is not an album for background listening — it basically demands your attention.

	“But as artists from Queen to Beyoncé have proven, ambition and excess can be glorious things when deployed with intelligence and humor, and while we’re not equating Raye with either of the above, there’s a similar sense here of trusting the artist to take you on an interesting voyage without wasting your time.”
	

	Performers at the show included Suede, Pulp, and others.

schema.headline: Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year

title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: ‘An Amazing Piece of Technology’ But ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’
description:
“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

	“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI F
body:
“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

	“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI Fest’s opening night U.S. premiere of “Wildwood.” “I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is a computer is technology. Technology is useful when you put it in the hands of people, when you put it in the hands of artists who can amplify their voice.
	

	“Technology is not useful when it takes the place of the artist, and that’s the concern with generative AI,” he continued. “It’s an amazing piece of technology, but the concern is that when it supplants the artist, then we have an issue because the computer cannot speak about humanity at all. It doesn’t know what it feels like.”


“Wildwood” director Travis Knight calls AI an “amazing piece of technology” but says, “I’m not embracing it at all.”“I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is technology. Technology is useful… pic.twitter.com/3SQQ87D2tq— Variety (@Variety) October 22, 2026


	“Wildwood” is a stop-motion fantasy feature about a young girl (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) who travels into a forbidden forest when her baby brother is kidnapped by a murder of crows. It took 16 years to complete the film, Knight said.

	“Sixteen years is a long time,” Knight said. “As I’ve said before, this film is old enough to have driven me to the premiere tonight. But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big sweeping adventure story. It’s a beautiful extravaganza. It’s an epic, but that’s not something that sustains you for 16 years.

	He continued, “At the heart of it, it has to be something that means something to you and that’s the thing I’m most proud of is that underneath it all, it is something that is really heartfelt, it’s beautiful, it’s emotional and that’s the thing I hope audiences take away from this.”
	

“Wildwood” director Travis Knight on the movie taking 16 years to complete:“Sixteen years is a long time,” Knight said. “As I’ve said before, this film is old enough to have driven me to the premiere tonight. But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big… pic.twitter.com/hNeDFa8mCc— Variety (@Variety) October 22, 2026


	Knight doesn’t believe that AI could have helped speed up the process — at least not if he wanted to maintain the highest quality. “That very notion fills me with rage,” he said. “Look, that’s the world we live in and the technology seems like it’s only pushing us in one direction, which is everything is going to be simpler. Everything is going to be automated; everything is going to be easier. What I would say to that is that there is something special about the human touch. There is something beautiful about humanity. And that’s one thing that stop motion represents. Stop-motion represents humanity at its finest creativity, emotion, care, devotion, time.

	“That’s something that AI could never do because a computer has never felt anything,” Knight added. “It’s never felt loss or love or pain, and that’s something that people can feel and that’s something you feel in something that was made by people.”



	

					“Wildwood”
									Courtesy of Laika
	



	The cast of “Wildwood” also includes Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Jake Johnson, Carey Mulligan, Maya Erskine, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg and Tantoo Cardinal.

	Bassett talked about recording her work during COVID. “I wanted to get out of the house, get creative again,” she told me. “It was just right on time.”


	See photos from the AFI Fest premiere of “Wildwood” below.

title: Laika’s First PG-13 Film, Brad Bird’s Neo-Noir and an Alzheimer’s Memoir: Animation’s Revolution Isn’t for Kids
description: The MPA gave “Wildwood” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and l
body:
The MPA gave “Wildwood” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and language,” which is a mouthful for any movie and an especially wild one for a stop-motion picture about a girl hunting for her kidnapped baby brother.

	It’s the first PG-13 in Laika’s 17 years as a feature studio, and at 130 minutes, it ties the record for the longest English-language animated film ever made. Travis Knight, who runs the Portland, Ore., studio and directed “Wildwood,” didn’t land there by accident. Anyone who remembers how dark the back half of “Kubo and the Two Strings” got probably isn’t shocked he went this far.
	

	Knight is one of the filmmakers taking part in this year’s Pixels and Pencils panel, Variety’s animation directors conversation at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, now in its fifth year. Joining Knight at the event are Brad Bird (“Ray Gunn”), Daniel Chong (“Hoppers”), Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado (“Forgotten Island”) and Leah Nelson (“Tangles”).


	The SCAD Savannah Film Festival runs Oct. 24-31.

	The panel has turned into a decent crystal ball leading to the Academy Awards. The director of “Flow,” Gints Zilbalodis, participated in 2024 before the little indie feature that could upset the big studios for the animated feature Oscar and last year, four of the eventual five nominees at the 98th Academy Awards, including winner “KPop Demon Hunters,” spoke at the event.

	Since “Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio” won the animated feature Oscar the 95th ceremony, the trophy hasn’t gone back to Disney or Pixar (“The Boy and the Heron,” “Flow” and “KPop” followed), which is a real shift for a category those two studios have owned since “Shrek” took the first trophy in the category in 2002.
	

	But this year, animation’s auteurs are making the movies they want to make.



	

					RAY GUNN — Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) and Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson).
									‘Ray Gunn’ ©2026 Skydance Animation
	



	Bird’s “Ray Gunn” is the easiest place to start, partly because the man has been chasing it since 1996, when a B-52s song and a Henry Mancini tune got tangled in his head and spit out a title. That was three years before “The Iron Giant” bombed at the box office (still a masterpiece, by the way) and then spent the next 25 years becoming the movie an entire generation of dads can’t get through without tearing up.

	He’s pitched his new film as “The Maltese Falcon” meets “Buck Rogers.” Sam Rockwell is Raymond Gunn, a gumshoe working a murder in Metropia, a version of 1939 that never happened, where humans and aliens share the same smoky streets. Netflix will release it Dec. 18, after London Film Festival screenings and a limited 70mm run. The PG rating comes with a note about “suggestive material,” which, if you know Bird’s work, tracks. Indeed, the Pixar licensing cash cow and family-friendly adventure “The Incredibles” was about a guy who hates his insurance job and misses his glory days.

	Chong’s “Hoppers” is the on the list our nieces and nephews have already watched twice on Disney+. The Pixar original opened to $46 million in March, the best start for an original since “Coco” in 2017 and cleared $500 million worldwide in about five weeks, which felt like the whole studio exhaling after “Elemental” and “Elio” stumbled out of the gate. Chong, who created “We Bare Bears” for Cartoon Network, made his feature directing debut with the story of Mabel (Piper Curda), a college student who uploads her mind into a robot beaver so she can talk to animals and keep developers from bulldozing their forest.

	It’s a family movie, sure. It’s also about habitat loss and how much people are willing to give up to stop it, and there’s a robot face removal scene that has reportedly sent some of the younger audience members out to the lobby. Timely, no?

	Crawford was on our very first panel back in 2022 with “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” the Oscar-nominated sequel nobody asked for that turned out to be a pretty frank movie about a cat who’s afraid to die. And people loved it. Mercado, his best friend in real life, co-directed that one too and their friendship, which goes back to “Kung Fu Panda 2,” is the seed of “Forgotten Island.”
	

	In the film, Jo (H.E.R.) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) grew up together in the Philippines in the 1990s and are about to be pulled apart, with Raissa off to Caltech and Jo staying home. Then they get stuck in Nakali, a place out of Philippine folklore that eats memories and if they don’t find a way out, they’ll forget each other entirely. You don’t need to have been 18 years old in Manila in the 1990s to feel that one. So seeing DreamWorks throw this kind of muscle behind a Filipino story with universal appeal means something.

	As for Laika, the studio is five for five in animated feature nominations, from “Coraline” to “Missing Link” and zero for five in wins, although “Missing Link” beat “Toy Story 4” and “Frozen II” at the Golden Globes.Knight, who got his own nomination for “Kubo,” directs the Chris Butler adaptation of Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis’ 2011 novel. In the stop-motion feature, Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) goes into the forbidden woods outside Portland after her brother is taken and stumbles into a war. The Laika crew built 136 sets and 231 puppets to get her there. Fathom releases “Wildwood” on Oct. 23, the day before Savannah kicks off.



	

									IFC
	



	Then there’s “Tangles,” which isn’t pretending to be anything other than a movie for adults. Nelson, a first-time feature director, wrote it with Sarah Leavitt, adapting Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s in the late 1990s. Abbi Jacobson voices Sarah, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus plays her mom and is among the producers with Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen.

	It got a seven-minute ovation at Cannes before Independent Film Company picked it up, and the charcoal-heavy animation does something with memory that live action could not pull off. The jokes are there early but the tears come fast and furious by credits roll.

	Both “Tangles” and “Wildwood” are also going drama at the Golden Globes, where animated titles have usually defaulted to comedy. It’s category paperwork, technically, but it says a lot about how these teams want their films seen.

	None of this is exactly new, by the way. “Persepolis” and “Anomalisa” were nominated by the Oscars years ago, and Japanese studios have been making animation for grown-ups for as long as we’ve been watching movies. Only three animated films, “Beauty and the Beast,” “Up” and “Toy Story 3,” have ever been nominated for best picture and the last of those was 15 years ago. What feels different in 2026 is the confidence. Nobody on this panel seems to be asking whether their story is “allowed” to be animated.
	

	They grew up on Saturday morning cartoons. Now they’re making them for Saturday night.

	This week’s updated predictions are below.

            Influencer Manuel Otto reportedly died by setting himself on fire during his livestream.
      
    
            According to local outlet PNP, the person who died in an attic apartment fire at Breitbrunn am Chiemsee is believed to be the 30-year-old owner of the apartment.
      
    
            While the outlet's English translation doesn't name the victim -- and says formal identification is pending -- The New York Post is reporting that it was Otto.
      
    
            The German outlet reports that one of the building's residents was able to extinguish the blaze ... but was not able to save the person inside the attic apartment.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As you know, Manuel -- who created the popular game Stick Run at just 14 years old -- died after an incident during a Twitch livestream.
      
    
            A spokesperson for Stick Run wrote in a statement that Otto "appeared to have taken his own life."
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            Twitch took down Manuel's livestream -- as well as his entire channel -- after the incident, with a spokesperson saying they acted fast to "prevent it from being viewed by others."
